extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory and philosophy of humour; writers and performers interested in the mechanics of comic effect
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical, literary and performative analysis of what makes things laughable and how comedic effects arise, with principles for identifying or producing comic elements in forms, movements, characters and situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is strictly human
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside the pale of what is strictly HUMAN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only human attitudes, expressions or uses make something laughable; animals or objects provoke laughter only insofar as they resemble or reflect a human attitude (e.g., laughing at an animal because it adopts a human expression; laughing at a hat because of the human shape/use it implies). Anti-pattern: treating non-human phenomena as intrinsically comic without reference to their human resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of feeling / disinterested spectator
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is accompanied by an ABSENCE OF FEELING; the comic demands something like a momentary anesthesia of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To laugh, one must be emotionally detached — sympathy, pity or strong feeling suppress laughter. Practical implication: comic effects work best when the audience is intellectually amused but not emotionally engaged. Anti-pattern: expecting laughter from scenes that simultaneously solicit deep sympathy or pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter requires an echo / is a group phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Our laughter is always the laughter of a group; laughter stands in need of an echo and is prolonged by reverberation among others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects are amplified by collective response (full theatre vs isolated listener). Some comic effects fail to translate across social groups because they depend on shared customs/ideas. Practical implication: consider audience membership and shared knowledge when crafting jokes or scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The social function of laughter: a corrective gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a sort of SOCIAL GESTURE whose function is utilitarian: to restrain eccentricity and correct inelasticity of character or behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson treats laughter as social 'correction'—it signals and discourages eccentric, mechanically rigid behaviour that threatens social cohesion. Implication for creators: comic ridicule often targets inelastic traits to encourage social adaptation. Anti-pattern: treating laughter as purely aesthetic without social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical inelasticity / automatism as core comic element
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element often consists of a certain MECHANICAL INELASTICITY — rigidity or momentum of movement, thought or character where flexibility is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a runner who falls because his muscles continue their previous motion; a victim of a practical joke who behaves like a machine; a person absorbed in past thoughts acting inappropriately in present circumstances. Practical test: if a person or action reads as 'mechanical' or 'puppet-like', it is likely to be comic. Anti-pattern: confusing mere oddness with mechanical inelasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The more natural the cause, the more comic the effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a certain comic effect has its origin in a certain cause, the more natural we regard the cause to be, the more comic shall we find the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic intensity increases when we can trace the behaviour to a believable, intrinsic cause (e.g., systematic absentmindedness rooted in a passionate preoccupation) rather than a random accident. Implication: build believable causes for ludicrous behaviour to heighten comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness / systematic preoccupation as comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: Absentmindedness — thinking of what one has done rather than what one is doing, or being absorbed in an imaginary situation — is a fertile source of comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types: transient absentminded acts (slipping) vs organised, systematic absentmindedness (Don Quixote-like figures). The latter can produce cumulative, coherent mishaps and a more profound comic character. Use: create characters whose inner fixation produces predictable, mechanical external behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vice: external, simplifiying, and unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The vice capable of making us comic is that which is brought from without — a ready-made rigidity that simplifies the person; comic characters are often unconscious of their defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes comedy from drama: comic vices retain a simple, independent existence and characters remain unaware (e.g., Harpagon). Practical implication: to create comic characters, present vices as external, stereotyped traits that the character fails to perceive. Anti-pattern: integrating the vice so deeply that it becomes tragic rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic physiognomy: imitatable deformity and fixed grimace
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity that may become comic is a deformity that a normally built person could successfully imitate; a comic expression is a unique and permanent grimace that 'promises nothing more than it gives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic faces suggest rigidity or stereotyped movement rather than mobile expressiveness. Caricatures exploit tendencies that a viewer could imitate. Practical test: if a normal person can adopt the deformity/pose and produce recognisably comic effect, it fits Bergson's physiognomic criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature principle: exaggeration to reveal latent tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature consists in detecting an imperceptible tendency in a face or form and magnifying it so the underlying grimace or mechanical tendency becomes visible; exaggeration must be a means, not the aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective caricature respects the 'ground plan' of the feature — it amplifies an existing inclination in the direction nature was already tending (lengthen a nose in its natural direction). Over-exaggeration without connection to an underlying tendency fails. Use exaggeration to make latent automatisms explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of gestures/movements: laughability proportional to machine-like impression
rubrics_metrics.description: THE ATTITUDES, GESTURES AND MOVEMENTS OF THE HUMAN BODY ARE LAUGHABLE IN EXACT PROPORTION AS THAT BODY REMINDS US OF A MERE MACHINE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A drawing or actor is more comic when the two images—person and puppet/mechanism—fit together clearly yet leave the impression of life. Practical implication: stage or draw characters to suggest internal mechanism while retaining semblance of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and predictability in gestures produce laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement that always the same, which returns at regular intervals and can be expected, diverts attention and evokes laughter because it appears automatic rather than alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a public speaker whose gesture repeats on cue; any repeated tic or pose. Use: controlled repetition can be used comically; anti-pattern: repetition that becomes annoying without irony or corrective framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation exposes automatism and is intrinsically laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation of gestures is laughable because it brings out the element of automatism present in the imitated person — gestures become imitable only when they cease to be fully alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical use in comedy: mimicry/parody makes mechanical elements explicit. Anti-pattern: faithful imitation of genuinely fluid, individual gestures will not be comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody device: connect gesture to a simple mechanical occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gestures become more frankly mechanical and therefore more comic when they are deflected (without changing form) toward some simple operation (e.g., sawing wood, striking an anvil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodic interpretation that maps a gesture onto a basic manual task heightens the machine-image. Use this technique in visual or physical comedy to increase clarity of the mechanical reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic is rigidity rather than ugliness; contrast with gracefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: If one contrasts the comic with its contrary, the comic should be contrasted with gracefulness more than with beauty: it partakes of rigidness rather than of ugliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on loss of suppleness and mobility (petrification of soul into matter) rather than mere unattractiveness. Anti-pattern: assuming anything ugly is comic; instead, check for the loss of adaptable movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as the outline of movement: immobile features suggest mechanical action
rubrics_metrics.description: In our eyes, form is always the outline of a movement; even parts incapable of movement (nose, ear) can be comic if they suggest a movement or convict of a fixed action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caricaturists alter shapes along the vector of implied movement to reveal a latent grimace. Practical implication: design visual comedy by exaggerating the implied motion in static features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental vs embedded comic: external trigger versus internal supply
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic may be accidental (brought about by an external circumstance: a stumbling-block or practical joke) or embedded in the person (when the person supplies by natural processes an inexhaustible series of opportunities revealing mechanical character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between isolated comic incidents and comic characters whose behaviour inexorably produces laughable situations. For sustained comedy, develop internal traits that regularly externalise as comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconsciousness of oneself increases laughability; self-awareness reduces it
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic character is generally comic in proportion to his ignorance of himself; a defect that is ridiculous, as soon as it feels itself to be so, endeavours to modify itself or appear differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve comic impact, present characters unaware of their ridiculous trait. If a character becomes self-conscious about the trait, comedic effect diminishes or shifts toward pathos/repair.
